title: The last kindness
hook: mourners shovel earth into the grave themselves

segments.voice: Yesterday was the funeral, and the prayer El Male Rachamim. Your line was god full of mercy. Who came to mind when you heard it? Today we stay at the graveside a little longer. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-two.

"And Isaac and Ishmael his sons buried him." That is how Genesis, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, closes the story of Abraham. Two brothers who grew up apart, one of them sent away into the wilderness as a boy, stand at the same grave. The text doesn't say they made peace. It says they buried their father. Jewish burial keeps that work in the hands of the people who loved the one who died. Once the prayers are said, the shovel does not stay with the cemetery workers. The daughter picks it up. Then the brother. Then the old friend from work. Earth lands on a plain wooden lid. It is slow, and heavy, and hard to watch. The tradition calls it a kindness. Today's word is that kindness.
screen: `ISAAC AND ISHMAEL AT ONE GRAVE.` → `THE MOURNERS TAKE THE SHOVEL.` → `EARTH ON PLAIN WOOD.`

segments.voice: The last kindness. Turn it four ways. First, the sons at the grave. Isaac and Ishmael bury Abraham. A generation later, Genesis tells the same of Isaac: his sons Esau and Jacob bury him, two more brothers with a hard history between them. Whatever lay between them, the burial was theirs to do. Second, the name. Earlier this week, with the holy society, we met Rashi's phrase for care of the dead: chesed shel emet, the kindness of truth, a kindness the one who receives it can never repay. Filling the grave is the last act of that kindness, and the tradition gives it to the people who loved the person, not only to strangers. It makes the death real. Nobody leaves the cemetery thinking it was a dream. Third, the small customs. In some communities the first scoops are taken with the back of the blade, so it doesn't look like ordinary digging. And when one person is done, they don't hand the shovel over. They push it back into the mound and step away, and the next person picks it up on their own. Some explain the back of the shovel as a sign of reluctance. Some explain putting it down as a way of not handing grief from one person to the next. Different communities give different reasons, and keep the custom anyway. Fourth, the circle around the grave. Not everyone holding the shovel is family. Friends and neighbors take a turn, because the work is shared. The person in the grave will never know who lifted the earth. No one is left to say thank you, and the shovel goes round anyway.
screen: `BROTHERS AT ONE GRAVE.` · `THE KINDNESS OF TRUTH.` · `NOT HANDED, PUT DOWN.` · `NO ONE LEFT TO THANK YOU.` · then, large: `THE LAST KINDNESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one hard kindness. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a kindness you've been putting off, not because it's big, but because it's hard. A call to someone who is ill. A visit that might be awkward. A job nobody will notice you did. Hold it there. If there's reluctance, notice where it sits, and let it sit. Then pick the kindness up the way a mourner picks up the shovel: once, with both hands, without waiting for someone to pass it to you. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
The last kindness. Chesed shel emet, the kindness of truth: care for the dead, who can never repay it. Today's word.
Your line: the last kindness. Today, pick up the hard kindness you named, before anyone has to hand it to you. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: At a Jewish burial, after the prayers, mourners and friends take turns placing earth into the grave themselves; in some communities the shovel is put back into the earth rather than handed from person to person.

trapdoor: what you thought: filling a grave is the cemetery's job.
what it means: the mourners do it themselves, as a last kindness to the one they loved.
what a scholar hears: Genesis 25:9 and 35:29 — estranged brothers burying their father — and Rashi on Genesis 47:29, chesed shel emet, a kindness no one can repay.

sources.quoted: And Isaac and Ishmael his sons buried him

notes: Genesis 25:9 fragment quoted as JPS 1917; confirm exact wording (KJV identical). Genesis 35:29 (Esau and Jacob bury Isaac) paraphrased.
Rashi on Genesis 47:29 paraphrased: kindness done with the dead is true kindness, since one does not expect repayment. Confirm.

Customs kept to 'some communities': using the back of the shovel for the first scoops, and returning the shovel to the earth rather than handing it on. Explanations given as 'some explain'. Confirm both are fair to describe.
